shortExplanation: The reciprocal square is one fourth.
detailedSteps: Because the negative sign is inside the parentheses, $(-2)^{-2}=1/(-2)^2=1/4$. Thus the expression is $2-1/4=7/4$.
keyIdeas: A negative integer with a negative exponent
commonMistakes: Treating the exponent as a multiplication or moving the sign outside the square.
difficultyNotes: Evaluate the parenthesized base before subtracting.

shortExplanation: Each task takes fifty minutes.
detailedSteps: The first two tasks take 100 minutes, so each of the three equal tasks takes 50 minutes. The third finishes 50 minutes after 2:40 PM, at 3:30 PM.
commonMistakes: Dividing the time for two tasks by three.
difficultyNotes: The known finish time belongs to the second task.

shortExplanation: Twenty-eight must occur three times.
detailedSteps: If 28 occurs twice, the other integer would be $(100-56)/3=44/3$, impossible. Therefore 28 occurs three times.
The other integer is $(100-84)/2=8$.
commonMistakes: Assuming without checking which value appears twice.
difficultyNotes: Integrality chooses the relevant equation.

shortExplanation: Hikmet occupies eighth place.
detailedSteps: Marta is sixth, so Jack is fifth. Todd is two places ahead of Jack, hence third; Rand is one place ahead of Todd, hence second.
Hikmet is six places behind Rand, hence eighth. David is two places behind Hikmet, hence tenth. All six stated placements fit the twelve-person race.
commonMistakes: Reversing ahead and behind when translating a rank difference.
difficultyNotes: Start from the one given absolute position.

shortExplanation: All thirty-seven extra games must be Shark wins.
detailedSteps: The largest possible Shark win count after N further games is N+1, out of N+3 games. Thus $(N+1)/(N+3)\ge19/20$ is necessary.
This inequality is $20N+20\ge19N+57$, so $N\ge37$. At N=37 the Sharks can win all additional games and finish with $38/40=95\%$, proving the minimum.
commonMistakes: Applying ninety-five percent only to the new games.
difficultyNotes: For a minimum, give the Sharks every available later win.

shortExplanation: Thirty-six of the 169 products are odd.
detailedSteps: The factors range from zero through twelve, so there are thirteen rows and thirteen columns. A product is odd exactly when both factors are odd.
There are six odd factors, giving $6^2=36$ odd entries among $13^2=169$. The ratio $36/169\approx0.2130$ rounds to 0.21.
keyIdeas: Odd factors in the full multiplication table
commonMistakes: Omitting the zero row and column.
difficultyNotes: The labels are not part of the table body.

shortExplanation: There are fifteen reflection axes and the rotation step is twenty-four degrees.
detailedSteps: A regular fifteen-gon has fifteen reflection axes, each through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite edge. The least positive rotation advances one vertex, so $R=360/15=24$ degrees.
Therefore $L+R=15+24=39$.
keyIdeas: Symmetries of a regular odd polygon
commonMistakes: Confusing the number of axes with the rotation angle.
difficultyNotes: Regular polygon symmetries are determined by successive vertices.

shortExplanation: The fourth root cancels the fourth power in 625.
detailedSteps: Write $625=5^4$. Then $(625^{\log_5 2015})^{1/4}=5^{\log_5 2015}=2015$. All bases are positive, so the real fourth root and exponent rules apply.
commonMistakes: Leaving an extra fourth root after the matching powers have canceled.
difficultyNotes: Rewrite the base before using the inverse logarithm rule.

shortExplanation: Two misses return the game to Larry’s turn.
detailedSteps: Let p be Larry’s winning probability. He wins immediately with probability one half. If both players miss, probability one fourth, the process restarts with the same winning probability p.
Hence $p=1/2+p/4$, giving $p=2/3$. The probability of infinitely many misses is zero because $(1/4)^k$ tends to zero.
commonMistakes: Treating alternating first-success opportunities as equally likely.
difficultyNotes: Independence makes each two-miss cycle identical.

shortExplanation: Exactly five side triples remain.
detailedSteps: Write the side lengths in strictly increasing order $a<b<c$ to exclude both equilateral and isosceles cases. The conditions are a+b>c and a+b+c<15.
If a=1, the triangle inequality is impossible. If a=2, then c=b+1 and the possible b values are 3,4,5, giving $(2,3,4),(2,4,5),(2,5,6)$.
If a=3, b=4 allows c=5 or 6; the first is the excluded right triangle (3,4,5). The other b possibility is b=5,c=6. Thus the two new triples are $(3,4,6),(3,5,6)$.
For a at least 4, even the least scalene perimeter is $4+5+6=15$, too large. None of the five listed triples is right, so the answer is five.
commonMistakes: Counting the right triangle (3,4,5) or a triangle with perimeter exactly fifteen.
difficultyNotes: Ordering the side lengths removes congruent duplicates.

shortExplanation: The legs are five and twelve, and the third altitude is sixty thirteenths.
detailedSteps: The axis intercepts are (5,0) and (0,12), so the right triangle has legs 5 and 12 and hypotenuse 13. Two altitudes are the two legs.
Its area is 30, so the altitude to the hypotenuse is $2\cdot30/13=60/13$. The sum is $5+12+60/13=281/13$.
commonMistakes: Counting only the altitude to the hypotenuse.
difficultyNotes: The right-triangle legs also serve as altitudes.

shortExplanation: Put nine in the variable counted with full weight.
detailedSteps: The left side factors as $(x-b)(2x-a-c)$, so the roots, including multiplicity, are b and (a+c)/2. Their sum is $b+(a+c)/2$.
To maximize it among three distinct digits, use the three largest digits 9,8,7 and assign the largest, 9, to b, which has the greater coefficient. The maximum is $9+(8+7)/2=33/2=16.5$.
commonMistakes: Maximizing each variable separately and violating distinctness.
difficultyNotes: The variable shared by both products has double the influence.

shortExplanation: The triangle ABC has two seventy-degree angles.
detailedSteps: Because C and D lie on the same arc side of chord AB in the cyclic quadrilateral, the inscribed angles ACB and ADB both measure forty degrees.
Triangle ABC therefore has $\angle B=180-70-40=70$ degrees. Its equal angles at A and B give $BC=AC=6$. The extra side AD is not needed.
keyIdeas: Equal angles yield equal cyclic chords
commonMistakes: Using a supplementary angle for ACB despite the cyclic vertex order.
difficultyNotes: Read the vertices in the quadrilateral’s cyclic order.

shortExplanation: The intersection cancels in the difference.
detailedSteps: If I is the intersection area, the requested difference is $(\text{circle area}-I)-(\text{triangle area}-I)$. It equals the difference of the two full areas.
The circle area is $4\pi$ and the equilateral triangle area is $(\sqrt3/4)4^2=4\sqrt3$. Thus the result is $4(\pi-\sqrt3)$.
commonMistakes: Computing the overlap even though it cancels.
difficultyNotes: A difference of two set differences removes their common region.

shortExplanation: English and History must contribute at least six points.
detailedSteps: The two certain As contribute eight points, so a GPA at least 3.5 requires at least six points from English and History. English C has probability 7/12, and History A or B has probability 7/12.
Condition on English: an A always succeeds, a B needs History A or B, and a C needs History A. Independence gives $1/6+(1/4)(7/12)+(7/12)(1/4)=11/24$.
keyIdeas: A total of six points from two subjects
commonMistakes: Adding subject probabilities instead of multiplying independent joint cases.
difficultyNotes: At least a C means there are exactly three possible grades in each uncertain subject.

shortExplanation: The vertical height is two root seven.
detailedSteps: The regular hexagon has circumradius 6. The common apex is equidistant from its six vertices, so its perpendicular projection is the hexagon center.
A lateral edge is 8, giving height $h=\sqrt{8^2-6^2}=2\sqrt7$. The hexagonal base area is $6(\sqrt3/4)6^2=54\sqrt3$.
The volume is $(1/3)(54\sqrt3)(2\sqrt7)=36\sqrt{21}$.
keyIdeas: Pyramid height from a vertex edge
commonMistakes: Using the lateral face altitude as the pyramid’s vertical height.
difficultyNotes: The vertex radius differs from the base apothem.

shortExplanation: Eleven is the unique listed solution; a zero-probability boundary remains.
detailedSteps: Every listed choice has n at least three, so both probabilities are positive. Their ratio is $\binom n3(1/4)^3(3/4)^{n-3}/[\binom n2(1/4)^2(3/4)^{n-2}]=(n-2)/9$. Equality gives n=11, choice D.

As a literal condition on all positive integers, n=1 also makes both probabilities zero. The source does not explicitly exclude this boundary. Thus 11 is the intended and unique listed answer, while an unrestricted uniqueness claim needs a clarified condition; the positive-integer solution set is therefore $\{1,11\}$, and only 11 appears among the choices. If zero tosses are permitted, $n=0$ also gives two zero probabilities; this additional convention does not affect the sole listed choice.
commonMistakes: Dividing the probabilities without checking that they are nonzero, or silently omitting the n=1 boundary.
difficultyNotes: The positive-event interpretation is clear among the answer choices but unstated for arbitrary n.

shortExplanation: Every integer greater than three is attainable.
detailedSteps: A composite integer has at least two prime factors counted with multiplicity, each at least two, so the sum is at least four.
For an even target t at least four, use $n=2^{t/2}$, whose prime-factor sum is t. For an odd target t at least five, use $n=3\cdot2^{(t-3)/2}$, also composite with prime-factor sum t.
These constructions realize every integer greater than three and exclude all smaller integers.
keyIdeas: Sums of prime factors with multiplicity
commonMistakes: Adding distinct prime factors only and forgetting repeated factors.
difficultyNotes: Multiplicity is part of the function definition.

shortExplanation: The right triangle must be isosceles.
detailedSteps: Put $C=(0,0), A=(a,0), B=(0,b)$ with a,b positive and $a^2+b^2=144$. The actual exterior squares give $W=(0,-a),Z=(a,-a),X=(b,a+b),Y=(a+b,a)$.
Write their common circle as $x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+F=0$. Subtracting its values at Z and W gives D=-a; subtracting its values at X and Y then gives $b^2+Eb=0$, hence E=-b.
Finally subtract its values at Y and W. The result is $ab+b^2+2Ea=b(b-a)=0$. Since b is positive, a=b. Thus both legs are $6\sqrt2$, and the perimeter is $12+12\sqrt2$.
Conversely these equal legs make all four square vertices lie on the circle centered at $(a/2,a/2)$ with squared radius $5a^2/2$, confirming feasibility.
keyIdeas: A common circle for two external squares
commonMistakes: Constructing a square inside the triangle and changing the cyclic condition.
difficultyNotes: Circle coefficient differences remove the unknown constant.

shortExplanation: The fifth row is constant one and every later row stays there.
detailedSteps: Write row i as the five values f(i,0) through f(i,4). From row zero $(1,2,3,4,0)$, the exact recurrence generates rows $(2,3,4,0,1)$, $(3,0,2,4,1)$, $(0,3,4,1,0)$, and $(3,1,3,1,3)$.
The next row is $(1,1,1,1,1)$. Substituting a constant-one preceding row into both recursive clauses yields the same constant-one row, so induction applies to every row i at least five.
Therefore $f(2015,2)=1$.
keyIdeas: A recursive row reaches a fixed state
commonMistakes: Using f(i-1,j-1) in place of the nested input f(i,j-1).
difficultyNotes: The previous row acts as a function, not merely a sequence shifted left.

shortExplanation: The possible stair counts total 193.
detailedSteps: For n stairs, the jump counts are $\lceil n/2\rceil$ and $\lceil n/5\rceil$. Their difference is 19. Since each ceiling differs from its argument by a number in [0,1), we have $|19-3n/10|<1$, hence $60<n<200/3$.
Checking the six integers from 61 through 66 gives only n=63,64,66, with count pairs (32,13), (32,13), (33,14).
The sum is $s=63+64+66=193$, whose digit sum is $1+9+3=13$.
commonMistakes: Rounding the stair counts down or excluding the shorter last jump.
difficultyNotes: A strict rounding-error bound makes the search finite.

shortExplanation: The three first-person destinations contribute six, eight and six completions.
detailedSteps: Label the original chairs zero through five. A person originally in chair i may move only to $i+2,i+3,i+4$ modulo six. Since the people retain their original identities, chairs are fixed and rotations are not identified.

Count successively by used destination set S. Starting with $T(\varnothing)=1$, add $T(S)$ to $T(S\cup\{j\})$ for each unused allowed destination j of person $i=|S|$. This exhausts each valid permutation once.
The first person’s destinations 2,3,4 yield respectively 6,8,6 completed assignments. Their sum is 20. A direct enumeration of all 720 chair permutations gives the same count.
commonMistakes: Dividing by six for circular symmetry even though the original occupied chairs identify the people and positions.
difficultyNotes: The restriction is relative to each person’s original chair.

shortExplanation: The reciprocal equation has ten ordered solutions.
detailedSteps: Dividing $abc=2(ab+ac+bc)$ by the positive volume gives $1/a+1/b+1/c=1/2$. Because $a\le b\le c$, this forces $3\le a\le6$.
For each a, positivity and c at least b give $2a/(a-2)<b\le4a/(a-2)$, along with b at least a. The third side is forced by $c=2ab/[(a-2)b-2a]$.
The finite bounds exhaust all possibilities, and each listed integer triple satisfies the original equality. The total is $5+3+1+1=10$.
keyIdeas: Integer boxes with equal volume and surface area
commonMistakes: Counting permutations of the side lengths despite the stipulated nondecreasing order.
difficultyNotes: Reciprocals provide both a finite bound and a forced third dimension.

shortExplanation: Noncongruent circles force one opposite-side pair and one same-side pair.
detailedSteps: Every center lies on the perpendicular bisector of PQ. Let the distances of the smaller-radius and larger-radius centers from R be u and v, with v>u. Since half the common chord is 24, their squared radii are $u^2+576$ and $v^2+576$.
The five-to-eight radius ratio gives $64u^2-25v^2=-39\cdot576$. Centers a distance 39 apart either have v-u=39 on the same side of R, or v+u=39 on opposite sides.

The opposite-side equation reduces to $u^2+50u-399=0$, whose positive root is u=7, v=32, with radii25 and40. The same-side equation reduces to $u^2-50u-399=0$, giving u=57, v=96, with radii $15\sqrt{17}$ and $24\sqrt{17}$.
If both pairs had the same case, two of the four radii would be equal, contrary to the source. Therefore one pair has each case, giving $AR+BR+CR+DR=7+32+57+96=192$.
These four radii are distinct, and centers at signed coordinates -7,32,57,96 on the bisector construct the required two pairs and common chord.
keyIdeas: Two radius ratios across a common chord
commonMistakes: Assuming the two centers in a pair must lie on opposite sides of the chord midpoint.
difficultyNotes: Different center signs produce two distinct admissible radius pairs.

shortExplanation: The distance is 1008 times the sum of root six and root two.
detailedSteps: Let $q=e^{i\pi/6}$. The jth displacement is $jq^{j-1}$, so after n flights the total is $S_n=\sum_{j=1}^n jq^{j-1}=[1-(n+1)q^n+nq^{n+1}]/(1-q)^2$, obtained by differentiating a finite geometric sum.
For n=2015, $q^n=q^{-1}$ and $q^{n+1}=1$. Thus $S_n=-2016/[q(1-q)]$, and its length is $2016/\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}=2016\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}$.
Since $\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}=(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)/2$, the distance is $1008\sqrt6+1008\sqrt2$. Both radicands are squarefree, so the requested sum is $1008+6+1008+2=2024$.
commonMistakes: Rotating the first eastward flight instead of only the later ones, or summing all flight lengths as the net distance.
difficultyNotes: A whole number of twelve-flight turns simplifies the nearly complete final cycle.
